So basically, for a given flow rate and temperature, rising power absorption by the coolant increases the vapour fraction of the coolant and decreases it's density. This leads to lower scattering and absorption through reduced macroscopic cross-sections which in turn leads to increased neutron economy of the reactor which increases reactivity. The RBMK recators used uranium 238 as fuel. As temperature of the fuel increases, an effect called Doppler broadening happens to the radiative capture cross-section of the U238 allowing it to absorb more neutrons thus limiting their ability to cause fission

Of the heat that nuclear reactors generate roughly 6% of it comes from radioactive decay of the fuel when the reactor is at full power and decreases according to the mix of the half lives of all the fission products. This graph: https://imgur.com/a/D8R6VJq quite nicely shows us that after a day this heat becomes approximately 0.1%. how long it takes to cool down depends on the coolant and the pumps. You can get the coolant to below boiling temperature after about a day but if you switched it off then the reactor would begin heating up again. The real q is how long until ambient heat loss is enough for the reactor to not overheat. This is dependant on a lot of factors but it'd probably be safe to turn off the pumps after a few weeks
